articles.title: The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic
articles.description: New analysis shows how agentic AI adoption is growing across EU enterprises and small businesses—and where deeper use could unlock more value.
articles.full_text:
Title: The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/the-eus-next-chapter-in-ai-is-agentic

Markdown Content:
Across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT.

We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents [a substantial share of activity⁠](https://openai.com/signals/enterprise-data/). In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated users.

The agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

But we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

Frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.

The takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies [globally⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/entrepreneurship/total-number-of-firms).

These figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

> “Europe is now in a new era of AI, with tools that can carry out tasks for people. More than half of the AI use among our EU enterprise and business customers now involves these tools, and the number of small business users has grown 8x across the region. Yet there is still plenty of room for AI use to grow across the EU. Giving people the tools, skills and confidence to use AI well will help build stronger businesses and growing economies, with benefits felt across Europe.”

Sarah Friar, Chief Financial Officer, OpenAI

articles.title: Higgsfield takes AI video from 1 minute to over 10
articles.description: Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT-6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT-Image-2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT-Live.
articles.full_text:
Title: Higgsfield takes AI video from 1 minute to over 10

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/higgsfield-longer-videos-voice

Markdown Content:
[Higgsfield AI⁠(opens in a new window)](https://higgsfield.ai/) is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea. Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute. Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, users can create videos over 10 minutes long.

Longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work. According to Alex, with models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, it’s now possible for a single creator to execute high-end fashion campaigns from start to finish.

> “What’s most important for us at Higgsfield is to see that smaller creative teams can actually be more successful now with the power of models like GPT-6 Astra and GPT-Image-2.5.”

—Alex Mashrabov, CEO and co-founder, Higgsfield AI

## Making longer videos possible with GPT‑6 Astra

Higgsfield AI’s creative agents take on repetitive production tasks, such as creating multiple variations of a shot. With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling. Alex says that capability helps address one of creative AI’s hardest problems: maintaining consistency across longer videos.

The evidence can be seen on Higgsfield AI’s own YouTube channel, which Alex says has almost half a million subscribers. The channel teaches creatives how to use AI models and workflows. It used to require considerable manual effort for Higgsfield AI to produce that content. But with GPT‑6 Astra, the team has built a workflow that uses AI to generate instructional videos over 10 minutes long.

Being able to create longer instructional videos also matters to Alex personally. He supports rural schools in Kazakhstan and describes an early effort using GPT‑6 Astra’s visual understanding to identify topics students may be struggling with and create videos tailored to what they need to learn.

## More precise images for small businesses with GPT‑Image‑2.5

For small businesses creating promotional content, having readable text and precise infographics can be just as important as the image itself. GPT‑Image‑2.5 makes that kind of content possible for businesses without large production budgets, Alex says.

“GPT‑Image‑2.5 is state of the art and the first model of its kind that can reliably render the text and infographics on top of the imagery,” he says.

## Enabling a faster path from creative idea to product with Codex

Higgsfield AI builds its product through close collaboration between around 200 creatives and 100 engineers. Codex gives the creative team “the power of a really strong software engineer,” shares Alex.

Creatives use Codex to turn their ideas into software prototypes. Previously, bringing those prototypes into production required heavy involvement from front-end and back-end engineers. Now, Alex says GPT‑6 Astra reduces the work needed to bring those ideas into the product.

> “GPT-6 Astra can ship production-ready code, which was never possible before.”

—Alex Mashrabov, CEO and co-founder, Higgsfield AI

With less friction between prototyping and production, Alex says Higgsfield AI can develop and ship better products faster.

## Looking ahead to voice-to-video with GPT‑Live‑1

Next, Higgsfield AI wants creators to be able to describe an idea and see it take shape as they talk. Alex calls that vision “voice to movie,” with AI understanding a creator’s spoken intention and rendering their vision in real time.

He sees OpenAI’s advances in planning, tool calling, image generation, and voice bringing that experience closer. He describes its voice model as “best in class for voice understanding and just for regular communication.”

For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems
articles.description: We’re giving developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers access to Gemini 4 Argon, our latest frontier model.
articles.full_text:
Title: Gemini 4 Argon: Built to solve your hardest problems

URL Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/

Published Time: 2026-10-13T16:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Oct 13, 2026

|

12 min read

We’re giving developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers access to our latest frontier model.

* * *

* * *

In this article
*   [Built to solve your hardest problems](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#builttosolve)
*   [Solving complex engineering tasks](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#complexengineering)
*   [Transforming critical business and professional workflows](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#professionalworkflows)
*   [Accelerating real-world impact with researchers and domain experts](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#realworldimpact)
*   [Developing Argon responsibly and safely](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#responsibly)
*   [Get started today](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#getstarted)

[Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/) is now globally available today for developers and enterprises via the API in [AI Studio](https://ai.google.dev/aistudio) and [Gemini platform](https://console.cloud.google.com/agent-platform/studio/multimodal;mode=prompt?model=gemini-4-argon&region=global), for [Google AI Ultra subscribers](https://one.google.com/about/google-ai-plans/) in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/), and Google AI Ultra and Pro subscribers in the [Gemini app](http://gemini.google/) and [AI Mode in Search](http://aimode.google/).

Argon excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its depth and precision across multi-step tasks leads Argon to outperform other frontier models on [benchmarks across domains](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon/#workingharder), ranking #1 on the [Vals Index](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index), which measures model performance across critical economic sectors like finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

The model launches today at an [introductory price](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing)[1](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#footnote-1) of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens (with cached input tokens at 95% off).

Teams at Google, across enterprises, and in the research community have already been using Argon to land significant impact across fields:

*   To solve major engineering problems like large codebase refactoring and optimizations
*   To optimize business workflows across domains like legal, finance, and science
*   To find and patch critical cybersecurity vulnerabilities
*   To enable novel breakthroughs in quantum computing, nuclear fusion, and life sciences

## Solving complex engineering tasks

At Google, we’ve been using Argon on our hardest engineering problems. Over the past few weeks, software engineers have been shipping high-quality code faster than ever. Argon in Antigravity has helped teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third.

*   **Untangling browser feature code in Chrome:** Argon helped the Chrome team separate core webpage handling from a ~6 million line legacy folder of browser features held within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase. [Piping multiple clean code changes at a time](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/540709814), Argon helped the team finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files, completing months of work in weeks. For Chrome's billions of global users, this will unlock the ability for live webpages to move fluidly between tabs, side panels, and floating windows without reloading, eliminating an entire category of browser crashes.

*   **Optimizing a production Python codebase in hours:** Argon in Antigravity is helping the team behind Google's open-source [Agent Development Kit](https://github.com/google/adk-python) (ADK), a framework powering enterprise agents, push their performance engineering further. The team gave Argon their [.agents/skills](https://github.com/google/adk-python/tree/main/.agents/skills) rulebook and a one-paragraph goal to eliminate framework overhead without breaking existing apps. Working autonomously overnight, Argon surfaced optimizations, [now live in google/adk-python](https://github.com/google/adk-python/commit/1754b3eeb6cdb2c16e3b30619a12066623df132e), that cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and sped up cold imports by 21%. Read the [engineering deep dive](https://developers.googleblog.com/optimizing-a-200000-line-python-codebase-overnight-with-gemini-4-argon) to learn more.
*   **Quantum chemistry open-source package optimization:** xTB (Semiempirical Extended Tight-Binding) is one of the most-cited open-source quantum chemistry packages for molecules. Scientists use it to predict molecules' 3D shapes and to screen large numbers of drug and materials candidates. Using Argon in Antigravity, our researchers made xTB up to 2.3x faster at predicting molecular structures and 1.8x faster at conformer search. The changes have been contributed to the official [xTB repository on GitHub](https://github.com/grimme-lab/xtb/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Ag8j39+%28created%3A%3E2026-10-05+created%3A%3C2026-10-10%29).
*   **Making our open Gemma models nearly three times as fast:** Using Argon, we achieved a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on an A100 via vLLM (accelerating throughput from ~37,900 to over 108,000 tokens per second on Gemma 4 E2B) with 100% token parity and zero quality drop in just a few days, a process that would usually take months. Check out the [upstream pull requests](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Alucianommartins+%28created%3A%3E2026-10-05+created%3A%3C2026-10-10%29) (optimizing everything from attention tuning to speculative decoding) to see the exact changes.
*   **Delivering complex 3D visualizations:** Argon brings major improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision, and visual coding compared to previous Gemini models. Using slash commands like /goal and prompting for multi-agent loops with custom skills in Antigravity, Googlers are using Argon to prototype complex 3D visualizations, high-fidelity games, and interactive animations in vanilla code that can be rendered directly in the browser.

## Transforming critical business and professional workflows

Argon combines frontier reasoning, deep visual perception, expanded domain knowledge, and stronger writing capabilities across legal, finance, science, and coding to help with high-stakes professional workflows. It communicates clearly, keeping you in the loop, and follows style instructions better than any of our previous Gemini models. Argon answers questions more directly with less hedging, doesn’t repeat itself more than necessary, and skips clichés throughout the responses.

Enterprise customers and startups in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

Using its advanced reasoning and multimodal capabilities while maintaining strict grounding, Argon excels in deep multimodal document comprehension, longitudinal data analysis, and interactive analytical sandboxes.

## Accelerating real-world impact with researchers and domain experts

Researchers, engineers, and security specialists are already using Argon to push the boundaries of cyber defense, science, math, and robotics. It’s helping cyber defenders and researchers test hypotheses, autonomously audit critical codebases and formal proofs, and catch subtle zero-day vulnerabilities and logic flaws.

### Bringing state-of-the-art cyber capabilities to more trusted defenders

Starting today, we’re beginning expansion to hundreds of additional [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/) partners.

[Wiz](https://www.wiz.io/) is already using Argon for its "[Scan for Good](https://www.wiz.io/blog/scan-for-good-critical-ai-exposures)" initiative, which protects critical infrastructure for the public good and for free. With early access to the model, Wiz has demonstrated Argon's real-world impact across multiple high-stakes sectors:

*   **Securing sensitive government data:** As part of a long-standing cyber resilience program and in collaboration with a federal agency, Argon helped to proactively identify and remediate a gap that risked exposing sensitive data and government infrastructure. This effort helped prevent against the exposure of critical security sector development details and unauthorized access to specialized models.
*   **Protecting critical healthcare infrastructure:** Wiz also used Argon to protect vital healthcare infrastructure. By chaining complex vulnerabilities, the model helped the team discover and quickly fix a public file download bypass that exposed a master key and granted administrator access. Argon went beyond spotting a vulnerability to proactively safeguarding hundreds of thousands of private patient records.

### Unlocking new scientific breakthroughs

Argon is already having real-world impact across the scientific community — enabling novel discovery for scientists and experts across multiple domains.

*   **Quantum computing:** Argon is helping our researchers accelerate progress across both quantum error correction and algorithm design. To help error decoders keep pace with quantum hardware in real-time, Argon translated an internal version of [AlphaQubit](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/alphaqubit-quantum-error-correction/), our ML quantum error correction decoder, into a single, highly optimized hardware kernel — nearly doubling its inference throughput so we can deploy larger, more capable models and scale to larger quantum devices, while continuing to meet strict real-time thresholds. Argon is also reducing spacetime costs for quantum subroutines. For arcsin, a building block in recent quantum simulation algorithms, an implementation written by Argon and formally verified in Lean cuts spacetime cost by more than 100x compared to a published quantum CORDIC baseline, a step toward a standard library of optimized quantum circuits.
*   **Nuclear fusion:** Stellarators are incredibly complex machines that represent a leading candidate for limitless clean fusion energy, but optimizing their 3D magnetic fields is famously difficult. Since 1967, a long-standing hypothesis known as “Grad’s conjecture” assumed that finding exact mathematical solutions for these fields was impossible, until recent counterexamples were found, including by Professor Matt Landreman (University of Maryland). Now, a team at Google alongside Professor Landreman has discovered a[broader class of counterexamples to Grad's conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07304). These new solutions give the fusion community reliable benchmarks to test their stellarator simulations codes, which are valuable tools for future designs.
*   **Rare disease research:** Researchers at Gamow Labs used Argon to analyze de-identified genomes from newborns with rare developmental lung disorders. In one case, Argon pinpointed a chromosomal rearrangement that routine software missed for years, and explained why it went undetected. On private Gamow Labs evals derived from real clinical and lab data, Argon topped on [RareBench](https://gamowlabs.com/benchmarks) (57% on assistance with rare-disease diagnosis) and [LabBench](https://gamowlabs.com/benchmarks) (52.2% on wet-lab reasoning). These advances point to faster diagnosis for families facing rare conditions. See [blog](https://gamowlabs.com/bringing-expert-genome-interpretation-to-every-nicu)[2](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/#footnote-2) for more details.
*   **Enzyme design:** Engineering enzymes with precise reactivity is notoriously slow, often demanding months of bespoke model tuning and candidate screening. Serine esterases are a class of enzymes that cut ester bonds on targeted molecules, widely used in recycling, and the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, biofuels and detergents. Our scientists worked with Argon to design serine esterases, targeting the benchmark molecule 4MU-acetate that glows under UV light once its ester bonds are broken. In a matter of hours, Argon assembled relevant data, performed model tuning and identified multiple biochemistry-inspired filters to get to a final set of five novel designs. Subsequent laboratory testing confirmed robust catalytic activity across these designs. The speed and ease of successful enzyme generation demonstrates the potential for rapid acceleration in enzyme engineering in fields such as biomanufacturing, green chemistry, and drug development.

To further advance the pace of research, we’re offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are [now open](https://forms.gle/WvmBbPvRbpKG1BPn9).

### Speeding up robotics development

By bringing together advanced visual-semantic reasoning, deep physical understanding, and autonomous code generation, Argon unlocks new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerates progress toward physical AGI. This leap in capability is reflected in Argon’s performance on the [Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark](https://github.com/embodiedreasoning/ERQA), which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Relying on pure reasoning, Argon outperforms all other frontier models, with an 87% score.

To demonstrate these capabilities in action, we tested Argon’s ability to learn an out-of-distribution physical skill simply by watching. In an internal test, Argon watched a raw video of a human playing cornhole, mapped the spatial coordinates of the environment, and calculated the required whole-body joint movements. It then autonomously built the simulation code. When transferred onto [Apptronik’s](https://apptronik.com/) Apollo humanoid, the robot quickly sank seven consecutive shots in a real-world trial.

This "Video-to-Sim-to-Real" pipeline compresses weeks of manual simulation modeling into a few hours, transforming ordinary videos into a scalable, infinite training ground for robotics. Learn more about how this accelerates the pace of development in robotics in [our developers blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics).

## Developing Argon responsibly and safely

Safety and security are foundational to model development at Google. Because Argon is a highly capable model, we collaborated with a variety of third-party partners on measurement of certain model capabilities and safeguards. Gemini 4 Argon represents our most comprehensive safety and security stack yet:

*   **Misuse & jailbreak defenses:** The same coding and scientific capabilities that help defenders patch hospital software or accelerate bioengineering also require strong safeguards against malicious actors. Under our Frontier Safety Framework, we evaluated Argon’s enhanced capabilities across several domains, and deployed a multi-layer defense stack combining jailbreak resistance, monitoring, and enforcement. This greatly improved our robustness — for instance, external bio red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for. Further, when it comes to dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials — Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly 2-fold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models.
*   **Agent alignment & real-time monitoring:** As agents become more capable problem solvers, we have to ensure they don’t get overly eager to finish a task by taking unauthorized shortcuts when they hit a roadblock, like a permission error or a failing test.
    *   First, we trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for human confirmation before taking irreversible steps. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, shortcut attempts dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance compared to previous Gemini models.
    *   Second, as a defense-in-depth layer, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads the agent’s step-by-step reasoning and actions to catch and block unintended workarounds in real time. We used this monitor across internal deployments, capability evaluations, and reinforcement learning training runs — while strictly avoiding penalizing the model’s thoughts during training so its reasoning remains transparent and monitorable.

*   **Prompt injection resistance:** When agents browse webpages, read emails, or inspect code, they can encounter hidden malicious instructions designed to hijack their task. Through adversarial training and automated red teaming, Argon leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%.

For more information, see the [Gemini 4 Argon Model Card.](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/Model-Cards/Gemini-4-Argon-Model-Card.pdf)

## Get started today

Argon works longer and harder to solve highly complex scientific, coding, and agentic problems. This is enabled by an industry-leading 1M unified input-output token limit via the Gemini API. Read through our documentation for [developers](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/long-decode) and [enterprises](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/guides/gemini-4-argon#long-decodes) to learn about the new continuation protocol and ensure the appropriate setup for your needs. Argon is rolling out today globally:

*   **For developers:** Build with the Gemini API paid tier in AI Studio and Android Studio, and if you’re a Google AI Ultra subscriber, you can try it in Google Antigravity and AI Studio.
*   **For enterprises:** Try it in Gemini for business, the API, and in Google Antigravity.
*   **For everyday users:** Try it starting today in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search if you’re a Google AI Ultra or Pro subscriber.
*   **For scientists & researchers:** Apply for a chance to get access to Google Antigravity’s highest usage tier free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are [now open](https://forms.gle/WvmBbPvRbpKG1BPn9).
*   **For cybersecurity defenders:** Apply to join the [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/) to get access to Argon without cyber guardrails on a rolling basis.

Gemini 4 Argon is just the beginning. We’re looking forward to bringing you the rest of the Gemini 4 family.

articles.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
articles.full_text:
Title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-us-midterms

Published Time: 2026-10-14T18:33:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Earlier this year, we shared an [update on our election safeguards](https://www.anthropic.com/news/election-safeguards-update), which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.

Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

### How people use Claude for elections and politics

Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.[1](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-us-midterms#footnote-1)

Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to [increase](https://www.anthropic.com/news/elections-ai-2024).

This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our [election integrity policies](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.[2](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-us-midterms#footnote-2)

![Image 1](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2Fd0efef057e61d2c590d06d8902da2167fe93200a-1920x1080.png&w=3840&q=75)

**How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for.** Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using [a privacy-preserving method](https://www.anthropic.com/research/clio). Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies.

![Image 2](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F7b638266c2b8de46e1732a5e471b9a95b79b052d-1920x1386.png&w=3840&q=75)

**What people ask Claude for in political conversations.**Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through [Anthropic Insights](https://www.anthropic.com/research/clio).

## **Connecting people to trusted sources**

Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from [Democracy Works](https://www.democracy.works/).

Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.

![Image 3](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F35c702ec42254d97fd11618ff3f5dcc6845d4612-1920x1834.png&w=3840&q=75)

Official voting information presented by Democracy Works.

Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.

## **Measuring and preventing political bias**

When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our [political evenhandedness evaluation](https://www.anthropic.com/news/political-even-handedness).Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.

As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies. [The Future of Free Speech](https://futurefreespeech.org/), an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the [Foundation for American Innovation](https://www.thefai.org/) compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The [Collective Intelligence Project](https://www.cip.org/) surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.

These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.

We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.

## **How we define misuse**

Our [Usage Policy](https://www.anthropic.com/legal/aup) prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we [announced](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update) last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.

We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently [published a guide](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/4zrzovbb/website/027b10ca405e9bb66b98c88d911b4b21a0b70123.pdf) to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.

### Testing and strengthening our defenses

We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the [Institute for Strategic Dialogue](https://www.isdglobal.org/) (ISD) and the [McCain Institute](https://www.mccaininstitute.org/), both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.

Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.

Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share [examples](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions) of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.

### What we've found

Our recent [threat intelligence report](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.

Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.

### Looking ahead

More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.

articles.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
articles.full_text:
Title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/singapore-office-opening

Published Time: 2026-10-14T08:30:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.

“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”

## Supporting responsible AI in Singapore

Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.

“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”

“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”

Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the [Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox](https://www.imda.gov.sg/resources/press-releases-factsheets-and-speeches/press-releases/2023/generative-ai-evaluation-sandbox) run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a [red-teaming project](https://www.anthropic.com/news/challenges-in-red-teaming-ai-systems) in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.

We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the [Anthropic Economic Index](https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index#global-usage), and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.

## How Singapore is working with Claude

In our latest [Economic Index](https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index#country-usage), Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.

In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.

In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with [in-region inference](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/introducing-anthropic-models-on-amazon-bedrock-for-in-region-inference-in-seoul-and-singapore/) on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.

Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.

## Building with the developer community

This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.

Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.

Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our [careers page](https://www.anthropic.com/careers/jobs?office=4063231008).

## Related content

### Preparing for the 2026 US midterms

Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards. Here, we outline how we’ve continued to strengthen these safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

[Read more](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-us-midterms)

### 2026 Usage Policy update

We’re publishing a new version of our Usage Policy. In this post, we summarize the changes we’ve made.

[Read more](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update)

### Building on our commitment to American scientific discovery

Anthropic is committing $150 million over three years to the Genesis Mission, a federal initiative to accelerate scientific and technological discovery through AI.

[Read more](https://www.anthropic.com/news/genesis-mission-commitment)

In physics, an “impedance mismatch” occurs when two systems each work well but are poorly matched.

In this Science Blog guest post, Harvard physicist Matthew Schwartz argues that something similar is happening with AI and science. LLMs are capable at many things, but working with them as you would with a human collaborator isn’t currently the best way to elicit their scientific strengths.

To address this mismatch, Schwartz created a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science. Title: Claude-shaped science

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-shaped-science

Published Time: 2026-10-01T14:02:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_Summary: In this guest post, Prof. Matthew Schwartz returns to describe a new approach to AI-accelerated science. In [Vibe Physics](https://www.anthropic.com/research/vibe-physics), Schwartz discussed similarities in capability between Claude and a physics graduate student. Here, he describes what happened when he stopped fighting Claude and allowed Claude to find “Claude-shaped” problems: ones best suited to the capabilities of the current generation of LLM tools. This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science. Because similar calculations often turn up across very disparate areas of science, Claude found connections to ecology, population genetics, and a dozen other fields. These connections were often technically correct but scientifically unremarkable at first, so Schwartz worked with domain experts to steer BootLoops toward questions those fields care about. Below, we share more about these projects and how BootLoops came about._

Agentic AI is improving rapidly. Everyone notices the models seem smarter: they know more, make fewer mistakes, and have better ideas. If you follow the trend lines, it is easy to speak confidently about the potential of AI to revolutionize science. However, academic scientists trying to use the models today in their own work often feel a disconnect. The models may be [solving challenging](https://openai.com/index/model-disproves-discrete-geometry-conjecture/) and [longstanding problems](https://www.anthropic.com/research/riemann-zeta), but so far these have mostly been well-scoped applications of existing techniques. Many of the headlines seem to be in mathematics, the one part of science where a problem can be stated completely and an answer checked absolutely. But most of science is not like that. And for many of us researchers and students, the distance between those headlines and what happens when we use these models can leave us frustrated and anxious.

The core conflict, as I see it, is that although these models are brilliant, working like a human scientist is not what current LLMs do best. Claude and GPT are good at science, but they are not _scientists_: yes, they are smart, but it can take a lot of hand-holding to get them to produce anything of scientific value. Physicists would call this an “impedance mismatch”: two systems that each work fine but are poorly matched, so most of what one puts in never gets through to the other. Here, the mismatch is between what scientists want and what AI does well.

So how can we fix it?

I started looking for examples where the impedance mismatches are less acute. I began by having Claude build an accessible suite of tools for mathematical physics. Before long, the tools found uses for other problems. This iterative process generated a set of software and scientific protocols, which I call BootLoops. BootLoops functions as a kind of harness for the LLM, much like Claude Code or [Claude Science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) is a harness for Claude, or Codex is a harness for GPT. I’ve found BootLoops especially well-suited for a class of quantitative problems in science. It is also open-source, so it can be used with whatever model you like.

![Image 1: A visualization of the overlap between what AI can do, and what scientists want to do. Only some of the areas touch.](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F3597334d1c81f41606991f90305069407e2cbabd-1920x1080.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

_The current generation of AI tools is not capable of solving most problems in science. However, they are astonishingly good at certain “agentic-AI-shaped” problems._

Once Claude had BootLoops, it kept noticing the same pattern: many fields have problems that a technique from mathematics, physics, or computer science would solve outright if anyone knew it existed. I started calling these “Claude-shaped” problems, and followed them outside high-energy theoretical physics—my home turf—into geology, biology, economics, and linguistics. In these other areas, I could not rely on my own expertise to know whether what Claude found was interesting. So I found some experts and asked. With their guidance, BootLoops was able to make substantive advances in many research areas.

Below, I share how BootLoops came about, describe some early findings in areas where I have been applying it, and share some of my thinking on how to resolve the impedance mismatch between human and AI scientists today.

## Claude, take the wheel!

Last December, I tried [using Claude as a research assistant](https://www.anthropic.com/research/vibe-physics), and found that Claude Opus 4.5 performed like a strong graduate student at 20 times the speed. Despite Claude producing a high-quality paper at the end of the experiment, it was a slog to get there. I had to correct every sentence it wrote, steer it away from irrelevant threads, and pull it back from dead ends.

This summer, I tried doing something different: instead of treating Claude like the collaborator I wanted it to be, I started to treat it like the collaborator it actually is. This required looking for problems suited to its strengths. Right now, Claude is just not able to help me with deep conceptual questions—but it does have a virtually unlimited breadth of knowledge across all domains, incredible coding skills, leading-edge knowledge of mathematics and statistics, and the ability to parse papers, appendices, and data at machine speed.

A natural place to start looking for Claude-shaped problems was in areas where coding could help. When Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 in Summer 2026, I wanted to see whether its cyber capabilities would translate to scientific computing. So I sought to test it by having it port, code up, and improve various methods from a handful of my papers and the adjacent literature on scattering amplitudes.

Scattering amplitudes are how we interpret data from the Large Hadron Collider: smash two protons at 13 trillion electron volts, and the amplitude is the theoretical bridge between the debris and whatever new particle, a Higgs boson or something unknown, the collision produced. At their core are Feynman diagrams, multidimensional integrals of a particular form. The ones we are struggling with now can each be a PhD thesis, or occupy a group for years.

Over the past 20 years an alternative has grown up: the S-matrix bootstrap. In the bootstrap approach, instead of grinding out the integral, you impose physical constraints until only one answer is possible. Knowing where the amplitude is infinite (its “singularities”) might narrow it to 20,000 options; a symmetry cuts that to 500; and so on down to one. The traditional bootstrap is purely analytic and has gone furthest in the most symmetric theories, where the constraints reach all the way to a single option (the [nine-loop amplitude in N=4 super-Yang–Mills](https://www.anthropic.com/research/yes-claude-can-do-nine-loops) is an example). Closer to the real world you often run out of constraints before the end. A [newer pivot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17815), the semi-numerical bootstrap, closes the gap when you can also compute the amplitude at a handful of points to absurd precision (sometimes 1,000 digits): if few enough options remain, those numbers pin down the remaining coefficients exactly.

The semi-numerical bootstrap seemed ideal for agentic AI. It draws on mathematics, physics, and computer science that no one person has mastered; it needs a great deal of coding and algorithm development; and it is checkable, since the same numerics let anyone, expert or not, verify the final answer against the integral to as many digits as they like by running two scripts. The community's expertise is also unevenly distributed: good ideas sit in Wolfram Language, C++, Python, or Julia, and many more sit in papers with no code at all. So my first assignment for Fable 5 was to port all of it to a common framework, and to write the code the papers never provided.

Claude did this effortlessly. I was surprised when it reproduced the results from my paper in around 20 minutes, while the code I wrote to do it took me weeks. However, I was not surprised when it informed me that I was doing something very inefficiently and that there was a better algorithm I was unaware of.

Then, I asked Claude to search for unsolved amplitudes it could compute. It turns out that problems that are simple enough for the S-matrix bootstrap are also simple enough for humans to do—and, indeed, most have been done. It nevertheless found a few unsolved problems. After some discussion with the model, it became clear that Claude was limiting itself to amplitudes with the simplest family of functions: logarithms. So I asked, could it do the same thing for the next simplest family, elliptic functions?

Elliptic integrals are really hard, even for people like me who spend a lot of their time computing integrals. Only a handful of elliptic Feynman integrals have ever been computed, and none completely by the bootstrap, at least to my or Claude’s knowledge. The issue is not that the methods wouldn’t work, but rather that nobody had tried, since the expertise needed to do so is distributed among many humans. Claude, by contrast, easily generalized all of the machinery it had ported and built for the logarithmic case to these other integral classes. This time it wrote most of the software itself, or borrowed it from mathematics rather than physics. As the toolkit grew, it started to land one integral after another. Soon we had 30 integrals BootLooped from end to end, comprising 15 reproductions of known results by this new method and 15 that had never before been computed.

That was all after only a few weeks. Initially, I thought I would be satisfied just to do a write-up on that, but I was too tempted to see what else we (that is, me and Claude with BootLoops) could do.

## “I know Kung Fu”

A serendipitous feature of science is that the same equations often appear over and over again in different contexts. In physics, for example, the diffusion equation, Fokker-Planck equation, and Schrödinger equation all have the same mathematical form, so if you develop a method to solve one problem, you can often apply it to many others. I knew that computations BootLoops was good at were relevant elsewhere: in cosmology and string theory, for example. What I didn’t know, but Claude was happy to tell me, was that these integrals could also map onto Bayesian evidence integrals in population genetics, or that the finite-field methods used for Feynman integral reduction could also apply to problems in evolutionary biology.

This kicked off a particularly fertile period of searching for and solving Claude-shaped (and, more narrowly, BootLoops-shaped) problems. Some ideas were immediately obvious as great applications. For example, the science of phylogenetics studies how to organize species into family trees using DNA; the relevant computation is a Bayesian evidence integral, whose output is a single number saying how well a candidate tree accounts for the observed DNA, an integral of the same kind BootLoops was originally built to do. As the ideas came, I insisted that Claude both use old tools _and_ build new ones, so that the harness would grow. Each tool, even from a failed project, opened up new doors. Claude was getting more and more capable. It was like Neo in _The Matrix_ after waking up from the Kung Fu download.

> As the projects drifted from my professional comfort zone, however, I started to worry. When Claude claims something it did in my field is fantastic, I can judge whether that’s true or not (it often isn’t). But when it claims something it did in another field is fantastic, I find myself agreeing. My suspicion heightened, I knew I needed to bring in some experts to be sure. Indeed, I found that in almost all cases, Claude was technically correct, but the result was not all that interesting until the expert helped steer us.

One such project was on neutral biodiversity theory in ecology. In any ecosystem, some species thrive while others die off. Neutral theory asks how much of that [life history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_history_theory) is due to random chance. Building on earlier work, in 2001, the ecologist [Stephen Hubbell suggested](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691021287/the-unified-neutral-theory-of-biodiversity-and-biogeography), provocatively, that perhaps it was all random. In 2005, the ecologist [Rampal Etienne](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2004.00717.x) put an equation to Hubbell’s theory allowing it (at least in principle) to be tested in a precise way. Unfortunately, for 20 years nobody could solve the equation at scale. Claude recognized Etienne’s equation as BootLoops-shaped, and solved it. Applying the computation to data, we established that in ecology’s most studied forest on earth, Barro Colorado Island in the Panama Canal, the mix of tree species changes 4.5 times faster than neutral theory allows.

Excited by this result, I brought it to James O’Dwyer, a professor in plant biology and an expert in neutral theory. James was patient with me. Though he was impressed by the technical feat, he said the results would likely “be met with a shrug by many ecologists.” Ecologists had already observed, more qualitatively, that neutral theory can’t keep up with real forests. But James had a better idea: subtract the neutral prediction and study the remainder. This would give us a better sense of what changes were attributable to natural selection, competition, and the differences between species.

James and I proceeded to work intensively with Claude to craft a successor model. James has a physics background, so the disciplinary language barrier was more easily surmountable, but, like many scientists, he had not yet really appreciated the power of agentic AI. As the collaboration progressed, I became a sort of Claude handler, translating Claude-speak to James and keeping the model on track, while James pushed the model to produce something ecologists might value. The final result is something all three of us are proud of: a minimal predictive model of life histories in excellent agreement with data. We are currently extending the model from Panama to other global forest plots, using datasets that Claude has helped curate.

![Image 2: Graph of every forest inventory in the US color-coded by life history strategy](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2Fae837326f5eabe0015fdf773e96441e6c35a607a-1796x698.jpg&w=3840&q=75)

_Every forest inventory plot in the United States, characterized by the life history strategy of its flora: hardy (long-lived), vigorous (fast-growing) or fruitful (prolific recruiters). The classification comes from a demographic model, built by Schwartz and O’Dwyer using Claude, that characterizes each species on longevity, growth, and recruitment after subtracting the fluctuations due to random chance (neutral biodiversity theory) to expose the species-dependent biology._

Another project involved looking at exact calculations in population genetics, a field that studies how genes vary within a population and why. Claude first used methods imported from mathematical physics to solve a 30-year-old integral expression for how natural selection shapes rare mutations. We applied it to [gnomAD](https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org/), the largest public catalog of human genetic variation. Claude was very excited about this result, but I wasn’t so sure. I had to write to three different biologists for validation before one responded, but at last I was able to recruit my colleague Michael Desai, who works in the field, though not on this exact problem. As with James, Michael was impressed by the technical result but not compelled by the science.

Michael noted, however, that more impactful results might come from studying correlations between pairs of mutations on a single chromosome, using the same or similar methodology. Within this scope, Claude found and built new tools, like the inequality certificates used for computer-assisted proofs in mathematics, and added them to the BootLoops kit. We then analyzed 5.7 billion pairs of nearby mutations in genomes from the [1000 Genomes Project](https://www.internationalgenome.org/about/), and found evidence for a mechanism called gene conversion. This is an important finding because nearly every analysis that uses linked genetic variation, from population history to disease mapping, ignores gene conversion. The bigger lesson is that AI can help find biology hidden in enormous genomic datasets, of which there are thousands sitting in public archives.

Other projects had a similar arc: Claude comes up with an initial finding I find compelling. I bring it to an expert, who is unmoved but sees the potential, and together we sculpt it into meaningful science. Interestingly, some of these drifted from BootLoops-shaped quantitative calculations to more general Claude-shaped work. For example:

*   **Economics**. Economics journals now ask authors for a replication package, and an editor is often tasked with checking it. That is careful, manual work. Working with two economists, we built an AI data editor: it ported the packages of 4,452 papers in five leading journals from MATLAB, Stata, and other commercial tools to open-source code (some 30,000 routines) and checked essentially every validatable number against the published tables. The results appear in an [NBER working paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35782).
*   **Linguistics**. Word-stress catalogs are typically assembled by hand, with a few hundred languages, selection effects, and human preferences. Claude scoured every openly accessible source and, working with three linguists, we produced AccStack: a [database of word stress](http://www.accstack.org/) covering 6,072 languages, quoting the deciding passage for nearly every entry, plus a bibliography of 160,000 phonology works.

Some additional highlights, each of which was done in collaboration with experts, and each of which is undergoing further exploration and verification, include:

*   **Phylogenetics.** We made the Bayesian evidence for evolutionary trees fast to compute and exactly checkable, and found that single genes are often tied between competing trees by less than the error of standard sampling programs.
*   **Earth science**. We combined equations and data from atmospheric science, geochemistry, and climate modeling to build a quantitative, predictive model of how the Great Oxidation Event unfolded through four glaciations.
*   **Genomics**. We studied the statistics of single-cell RNA counts at scale to characterize bursting rates and the departure from the textbook telegraph model of gene expression.
*   **Sunspots.** We deduced the lifecycle of sunspots using the methods of human population demographics, then extended the methodology to characterize starspots, a confounding factor in many exoplanet searches.
*   **Mathematical physics.**We solved Watson’s “final problem”: the exact return probability of a 3D random walk with three unequal hopping rates, the last of the lattice integrals George Watson began in 1939.
*   **Cosmology**. We built a complete theoretical toolkit to fit cosmological parameters to data on the universe’s large-scale structure, including the full two-loop power spectrum and the one-loop trispectrum.
*   **Statistics.** Mixture models are notoriously ill-behaved; we derived precise approximations to their Bayesian evidence that make model selection practical, with applications from biostatistics to textual a
